topicos.aulaTitulo: Sounds and first words
topicos.titulo: Long and short vowels, and vowel pairs
topicos.explicacao: Some letters together make a sound of their own. The rule always holds. STEP 1: listen to «Tal» and then «Ball». In «Tal» the vowel «a» is long, as if you stretched it: «tahl». In «Ball» it is short. STEP 2: after a vowel, a single consonant usually leaves the vowel long, as in «Name». Two consonants leave it short, as in «Kette». STEP 3: two vowels together make a new sound. The pair «ei» sounds «eye», and «Eis» is read «ice». STEP 4: the pair «ie» is a long «ee», and «Bier» is read «beer». STEP 5: the pairs «eu» and «äu» sound «oy», and «Euro» is read «OY-roh». STEP 6: the pair «au» sounds «ow», as in «house», and «Haus» is read «howss». Be careful not to mix them up: «ei» sounds «eye», but «ie» sounds «ee».
topicos.comparacao: in English the letters «ei» would be read «ay», as in «eight». In German «ei» sounds «eye», as in «ice». The pair «ie» is not the English «ie» of «pie»: it is a long «ee».

erros.motivo: German «ei» sounds «eye», as in «ice». The word is read «ice».
The pair «ie» is a long «ee». The word is read «beer», with no separate «e» sound.
The pair «eu» sounds «oy». The word is read «OY-roh».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Sounds and first words
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the group «sch» sounds «sh», as in «shoe». The word «Schule» is read «SHOO-leh». STEP 2: at the start of a word, «sp» and «st» sound «shp» and «sht». «Sport» is read «shport» and «Stein» is read «shtine». STEP 3: the group «ch» has two sounds. After «e», «i», «ä», «ö», «ü», «l», «n» and «r» it is soft: a very light stream of air, like a whispered «h» in «hue». «Ich» is read «ikh». STEP 4: after «a», «o», «u» and the pair «au», «ch» is rough: it comes from the back of the throat, as in Scottish «loch». «Buch» is read «bookh». STEP 5: the group «tsch» sounds «ch», as in «church». «Deutsch» is read «doitch». STEP 6: the group «pf» joins «p» and «f» in a single breath: «Apfel». The group «qu» sounds «kv»: «Quelle». The group «ck» is a short «k»: «Jacke». The group «ng» is nasal, with no separate «g» at the end: «singen».
topicos.comparacao: in English «ch» sounds «tch», as in «chair». In German «ch» is another sound, soft or rough, and the «sh» sound is written «sch».

erros.motivo: The group «sch» always sounds «sh». The word is read «SHOO-leh».
At the start of a word, «sp» sounds «shp». The word is read «shport».
After «u», «ch» is rough, as in Scottish «loch». The word is read «bookh».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Sounds and first words
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «Hallo» and «Tschüs» are for friends and colleagues, at any time of day. STEP 2: «Guten Morgen» is said in the morning, «Guten Tag» during the day and «Guten Abend» in the evening, on arrival. STEP 3: «Gute Nacht» is different. It is only said when leaving, before sleeping. STEP 4: to ask how someone is, say «Wie geht’s?», read «vee gayts». Answer «Gut, danke!». STEP 5: «Danke» means thank you, for a man or a woman. In German the word is the same.
topicos.comparacao: in English «good night» works both on arrival and before sleeping. In German there are two expressions: «Guten Abend» on arrival and «Gute Nacht» before sleeping.

erros.errado: Gute Nacht, arriving at a party in the evening
erros.motivo: «Gute Nacht» is only said when leaving, to someone who is going to sleep. On arrival, say «Guten Abend».

erros.errado: Guten Tag, at eight in the evening
erros.motivo: In the evening the greeting changes to «Guten Abend». «Guten Tag» is for the day.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Who I am
topicos.titulo: Word order and your first questions
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: listen to «Ich heiße Lea.» and then «Wie heißt du?». To say your name, the verb is «heißen», "to be called" — German says "I am called Lea", not "my name is". STEP 2: in German, the conjugated verb is always in SECOND position in the sentence. In «Ich heiße Lea», «ich» takes first position and «heiße» second. STEP 3: in questions with a question word, that word comes first. Examples: «wie», which means "how" and sounds like «vee», and «woher», which means "where from" and sounds like «voh-HEHR». The verb stays second: «Wie heißt du?» and «Woher kommst du?». STEP 4: in a yes/no question, the verb moves to the front: «Heißt du Lea?» — no "do" needed, unlike English. Answer «Ja» or «Nein». STEP 5: the verb ending changes with the person. With «ich», it ends in «e»: «ich heiße», «ich komme». With «du», it ends in «st»: «du kommst». In «heißen», the «ß» already makes the «s» sound, so you only add «t»: «du heißt». STEP 6: as in English, the pronoun is required: «Ich komme aus den USA», never just «Komme aus den USA». STEP 7: a heads-up. In «der Name» and «der Vorname», «der» is an article (a German "the"). You'll learn the articles in lesson 3. For now, repeat «der» together with the word.
topicos.comparacao: English and German start out alike: «Ich heiße Lea», "I am called Lea". The difference shows up as soon as something else opens the sentence. English keeps subject-then-verb ("Today I come"), but German keeps the verb in second place no matter what comes first: «Heute komme ich», literally "Today come I". English has a trace of this in questions ("Where are you from?"), and German questions work the same way: «Woher kommst du?». One more trap: «Wer» means "who", not "where" — "where" is «wo».

linhas.pt: What's your name? My name is Anna.
What's your name? (formal) My name is Müller.
Where are you from? I'm from Brazil.
Where are you from? (formal) I'm from Brazil.

erros.motivo: The conjugated verb goes in second position, right after «ich».
In a question with «wie», the verb comes right after the question word.
The pronoun «ich» can never be dropped, just like "I" in English.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Who I am
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: German "to be" is «sein», pronounced «zine». STEP 2: «sein» is irregular and changes a lot, just like "am, are, is". Listen to the forms: «ich bin», «du bist», «er, sie, es ist», «wir sind», «ihr seid», «sie sind». Careful: «sind» sounds like «zint» and «seid» like «zite». STEP 3: use «sein» to say who you are: «Ich bin Amerikaner» or «Das ist Lea». STEP 4: use it also to say how or where you are: «Ich bin müde» and «Wir sind hier». STEP 5: to make it negative, put «nicht» after the verb: «Ich bin nicht müde» — like "I am not tired". STEP 6: in a yes/no question, the verb moves to the front: «Bist du müde?», "Are you tired?". Answer: «Ja, ich bin müde.» or «Nein, ich bin nicht müde.»
topicos.comparacao: «sein» is the German "to be", and it behaves almost exactly like it: one verb for who you are and how or where you are, irregular in every person, just as "am, are, is" are. Match them up and they stick: «ich bin» (I am), «du bist» (you are), «er ist» (he is). One trap: German says «Ich bin müde» (I'm tired), but for cold, hunger and age it often switches verbs — «Mir ist kalt», not «Ich bin kalt», which would mean you're a cold person. You'll meet those later.

erros.motivo: Each person has its own form. With «ich», it's always «bin».
With «wir», the form is «sind». «Ist» goes with «er», «sie» and «es».
The verb stays in second position, and «nicht» comes after it.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Who I am
topicos.titulo: Three ways to say "you": du, ihr and Sie
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to talk to ONE person you're close to — a friend, family member, child or young classmate — use «du». STEP 2: to talk to SEVERAL people you're close to, use «ihr», like "you guys" or "y'all". STEP 3: to talk to someone you don't know well, or to show respect, use «Sie», pronounced «zee». It covers sir, ma'am, and any group addressed formally. In writing, formal «Sie» always starts with a capital S. STEP 4: with «Sie» the verb takes the same form as «sie» (they): «Sie sind» and «Wie heißen Sie?». STEP 5: when in doubt, use «Sie». The other person will offer you «du» when they want to — and in German that's a real moment, not a formality.
topicos.comparacao: English has one "you" for everyone. German has three, and the choice is not optional: «du» for one friend, «ihr» for several (like "you guys" or "y'all"), and «Sie» for anyone you'd call Mr. or Ms. Using «du» with a stranger, a shop clerk or your boss sounds rude in Germany. And the choice changes the verb: «Wie heißt du?» but «Wie heißen Sie?».

erros.motivo: With «Sie» the verb is plural, even for one person.
With «du», the form of «sein» is «bist». «Sind» goes with «wir» and «sie».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Who I am
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to say where you're from, use «Ich komme aus» and the country: «Ich komme aus Kanada». STEP 2: most countries take no article: «Kanada», «England», «Deutschland». A few do, and you learn them as fixed phrases: «Ich komme aus den USA», «Ich komme aus der Schweiz». You'll understand why later. STEP 3: for a man's nationality, use «Amerikaner». For a woman, add «in»: «Amerikanerin». STEP 4: after «sein», the nationality takes no article — unlike English "I'm an American": «Ich bin Amerikaner». STEP 5: languages take no article either, and they're capitalized, as in English: «Ich spreche Deutsch». STEP 6: the verb «sprechen» (to speak) is irregular with «du» and «er»: «ich spreche», «du sprichst», «er spricht». The «sp» at the start sounds like «shp», as you saw in lesson 1.
topicos.comparacao: English often uses one word for the person and the language ("German", "Spanish"). German keeps three apart: the country «Deutschland», the person «Deutscher / Deutsche», and the language «Deutsch». Two English habits to drop: no article before a nationality — "I'm an American" is «Ich bin Amerikaner», never «ein Amerikaner» — and a woman adds «-in»: «Amerikanerin», «Engländerin», «Kanadierin».

exemplos.ru: Ich komme aus Brasilien. Ich bin Brasilianer.
Sie kommt aus Deutschland. Sie ist Deutsche.

erros.motivo: For nationality, German uses no article — unlike English "I'm an American".
For a woman, the word takes the ending «in».
The language has its own form, with no ending: «Deutsch».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: English has one word for "the". German has three, one per gender: der (masculine), die (feminine) and das (neuter). In the plural, it's always die. STEP 2: English calls every object "it". German doesn't: a thing is «er», «sie» or «es» depending on its gender — «Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist modern.» STEP 3: so never learn Tisch. Learn der Tisch.
topicos.comparacao: Old English had genders too — modern English dropped them, German kept them. That's why the gender of a German noun can't be guessed from its meaning: a table is masculine, a lamp feminine, a girl («das Mädchen») neuter. The gender is part of the word, and the only safe way is to learn it together with the word, as one unit.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.titulo: Der, die, das: the three genders
topicos.explicacao: In German every noun has a gender: masculine (der), feminine (die) or neuter (das). Gender is grammar, not meaning: «das Mädchen» (the girl) is neuter. So always memorize the article with the word. EVERY noun is written with a CAPITAL letter, anywhere in the sentence — not just names, as in English. Endings give clues, with exceptions: -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tion, -ie and most words in -e are feminine; -er, -ling and -ismus are masculine; -chen, -lein, -um and -ment are neuter. Days of the week, months and seasons are masculine. Handy English link: -heit and -schaft often match English -hood and -ship (die Kindheit = childhood, die Freundschaft = friendship).
topicos.comparacao: English only keeps gender in he/she/it for people and animals. German assigns a gender to every noun, and it rarely matches what you'd expect: «das Kind» (the child) is neuter, «die Person» is feminine even for a man.

linhas.exemplo: der Mann, der Tisch, der Vater
die Frau, die Lampe, die Mutter
das Kind, das Buch, das Haus
die Zeitung, die Freiheit, die Nation, die Familie, die Lampe
das Mädchen, das Museum, das Dokument
der Montag, der Juli, der Sommer

erros.motivo: Kind is neuter, and nouns are capitalized.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: look at the endings of the words in each group. STEP 2: Group A: die Zeitung, die Wohnung, die Gesundheit, die Möglichkeit, die Freundschaft, die Information. STEP 3: Group B: das Mädchen, das Brötchen, das Büchlein, das Instrument. STEP 4: Group C: der Lehrer, der Computer, der Frühling, der Montag, der Dezember. STEP 5: which endings mark group A and group B? What does group C have in common, besides the ending? STEP 6: now look at the plurals:

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.explicacao: German plurals come in five patterns: -e (der Tisch → die Tische), -(e)n (die Lampe → die Lampen), -er (das Buch → die Bücher), no ending (der Lehrer → die Lehrer) and -s (das Auto → die Autos, common in foreign words). Many words also add an umlaut to the vowel (a → ä, o → ö, u → ü) — just like English man → men, foot → feet, mouse → mice, which are leftovers of the same old Germanic rule. There's no safe rule: learn the plural with the noun. The plural definite article is always «die», for all three genders.
topicos.comparacao: The English reflex is to add -s. In German, -s is the rarest pattern (mostly foreign words: Autos, Hotels). English already has the German patterns in its oldest words: child → children is the German -er (Kind → Kinder), ox → oxen is -en, man → men is the umlaut (Mann → Männer).

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.explicacao: «Ein» and «eine» are the German "a/an": ein Mann, eine Frau, ein Kind. Half the guesswork disappears with one rule: «ein» is for der and das words, «eine» only for die words. As in English, there's no "a" in the plural: «Das sind Bücher» (those are books). To negate a noun, German uses «kein» (or «keine»), with the same endings as «ein»: «Das ist kein Tisch» = "that's not a table" / "that's no table". To point at things, use «das ist» for one and «das sind» for several — «das» here works like English "that", whatever the gender.

erros.motivo: There's no "a" in the plural, just like in English.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Nouns and articles
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest habits come straight from English: one "the" for everything (die Tisch instead of der Tisch), "it" for every thing (es for der Tisch instead of er), the English -s plural (die Kinds), and "a" before a job (Ich bin eine Lehrerin, from "I'm a teacher"). STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: Tisch is masculine (der Tisch), so "a" is ein. Only die words take eine.

erros.errado: Der Tisch ist neu. Es ist modern.
erros.certo: Der Tisch ist neu. Er ist modern.
erros.motivo: English says "it" for every thing; German uses the noun's gender: der Tisch → er.
Not the English -s: Kind → Kinder, just like child → children.
No article before a job after sein — unlike "I'm a teacher".
In a compound, the last part decides the gender: die Tasse → die Kaffeetasse.
Every German noun is capitalized, not just names.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: count the positions. One block, then the verb. Always in that order.
topicos.comparacao: In English, the subject sticks to the verb: "Today I live in Munich." Copy that into German and you get Heute ich wohne in München, which is wrong. In German, the verb never leaves second position. When anything other than the subject opens the sentence, the subject moves to after the verb: Heute wohne ich in München — literally "Today live I in Munich". English still does this in a few fixed phrases ("Here comes the bus", "Never have I seen…"); German does it all the time.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.explicacao: Almost all German verbs end in -en in the infinitive. Drop the -en to find the stem and add the endings: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en. Where English adds only one -s ("he works"), German changes for every person — but there are only five endings to learn. If the stem ends in -t or -d (arbeiten, finden), an extra -e- goes in before -st and -t, to make it pronounceable: du arbeitest, er arbeitet. If the stem ends in -s, -ß or -z (heißen, reisen), «du» loses the -s of its ending: du heißt, du reist. The «wir», «sie» and «Sie» forms are the same as the infinitive.
topicos.comparacao: English marks only one person in the present (he/she/it works). German marks almost all of them, but the pattern is short and regular, and «wir», «sie» and «Sie» simply repeat the infinitive. Good news: German has no "do" in questions or negatives and no -ing form — «Ich lerne» covers "I learn", "I'm learning" and "I do learn".

erros.motivo: Stem in -s: «du» loses the -s of the ending.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: read the four sentences and notice where the verb and the subject are. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: which word never moves in any of the four? STEP 4: what happens to Tom when something else opens the sentence? STEP 5: in sentence 4, how many words come before the verb?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.titulo: Verb in second position, questions and negatives
topicos.explicacao: The conjugated verb always sits in 2nd position. If the sentence starts with something else (today, tomorrow), the subject moves to after the verb: «Heute arbeite ich.» In yes/no questions, the verb comes 1st — no "do" needed: «Wohnst du in Berlin?» (Do you live in Berlin?). In questions with a question word, the word comes 1st and the verb 2nd: «Wo wohnst du?» The negative «nicht» goes after the verb («Ich arbeite nicht» = I don't work) or before what it negates («Ich wohne nicht in Berlin»). To say you like doing something, put «gern» after the verb: «Ich lerne gern Deutsch» (I like learning German).

erros.motivo: The conjugated verb goes in 2nd position.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Present tense verbs and word order
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest mistake is keeping the subject glued to the front after a time or place word: Heute ich lerne. It feels natural because English does it ("Today I learn"), but in German the verb is a magnet fixed in position 2 and the subject moves after it (inversion). Two more English habits: adding a "do" (there is none: «Wohnst du hier?») and translating "I am learning" word for word (just «Ich lerne»). STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: The verb stays in position 2; the subject moves after it — not "Today I learn".
Any time word in position 1 pushes the subject after the verb.
German has no "do": the verb itself opens a yes/no question.
No "am …-ing" in German: «Ich lerne» already means "I'm learning".
Stem in -t: add an -e- before the ending.
«gern» goes right after the verb, before the object.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: good news first: German possessives work like English ones — no article before them. "My father" is mein Vater, never der mein Vater. STEP 2: the owner picks the stem (my → mein, his → sein, her → ihr); the thing owned picks the ending (mein Vater, meine Mutter).
topicos.comparacao: English already gets the owner right: "his father", "her father". German does the same with sein and ihr. The difference: the German possessive also takes an ending that agrees with the thing owned — something English never does. So "his mother" is seine Mutter and "her father" is ihr Vater. And watch the triple meaning of ihr: «ihr» = her / their, «Ihr» (capital) = your (formal), and «ihr» = you all.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.explicacao: «Haben» (to have) is irregular. The direct object of «haben» goes into the accusative. In the masculine singular, «ein» becomes «einen» and «kein» becomes «keinen»; in the feminine, neuter and plural nothing changes: «Ich habe einen Bruder. Ich habe eine Schwester. Ich habe ein Kind. Ich habe keine Kinder».
topicos.comparacao: English shows the same idea only in pronouns: "he" sees, but you see "him". German does it with articles too, but only for masculine nouns: «ein Bruder» (the one who is) becomes «einen Bruder» (the one you have) — like he → him.

tabelas.titulo: The accusative only changes the masculine

erros.motivo: To negate a noun, use kein/keine — not "nicht ein".

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: look at the endings of mein. STEP 2: now look at the owner. STEP 3: Tom und seine Mutter. Lena und ihr Vater. STEP 4: Camila und ihr Bruder. STEP 5: Questions: STEP 6: which words you already know do the endings of mein remind you of? STEP 7: what decides between sein and ihr? STEP 8: what decides between seine and sein?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.explicacao: Possessives agree with the THING owned (gender and number), in their ending: «mein Vater», «meine Mutter», «mein Kind», «meine Eltern». They take the same endings as «ein»: no ending for masculine and neuter, -e for feminine and plural. The stem comes from the owner, as in English: «sein» = his (or its), «ihr» = her (and their); «Ihr», capitalized, is the formal "your". Careful: «unser» and «euer» lose the inner -e- before an ending: unsere, eure.

erros.motivo: «sein» = his; «ihr» = her — exactly as in English.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.explicacao: From 13 to 19, numbers are built with the base + «-zehn», just like English "-teen": dreizehn (thirteen), vierzehn, fünfzehn… Careful: 16 = sechzehn (drops the -s) and 17 = siebzehn (drops the -en). 11 (elf) and 12 (zwölf) are special — compare eleven and twelve; 20 is zwanzig. To give your age: «Ich bin zwanzig Jahre alt» or just «Ich bin zwanzig» — the same "to be" as English "I'm twenty".

topicos.aulaTitulo: Family, haben and possessives
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: English speakers get the owner right (his → sein, her → ihr) but forget the ending: sein Mutter instead of seine Mutter. Other costly habits: "a brother" as object staying ein Bruder instead of einen Bruder, and "I have not children" as nicht Kinder instead of keine Kinder. STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: The owner is right ("his"), but the ending must agree with Mutter (feminine): seine.
The owner is Lena, so "her": ihr — exactly as in English.
No article before a possessive, as in English "my brother".
Masculine direct object: ein → einen (like he → him).
"Not any / no" before a noun is kein(e), not nicht.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: halb looks ahead to the next hour. Halb vier is half an hour BEFORE four: 3:30, not "half four".
topicos.comparacao: Four traps are waiting for English speakers — and one of them can make you an hour late.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.explicacao: From 21 to 99, German says the ones first and then the tens, joined by «und»: 25 = fünfundzwanzig, "five-and-twenty" — like the old English "four-and-twenty blackbirds". «Eins» becomes «ein»: 21 = einundzwanzig. And it's all one word. Watch 16 and 60 (sechzehn, sechzig) and 17 and 70 (siebzehn, siebzig): they drop letters. 30 is dreißig, with ß. Hundreds simply add up: zweihundert (200), 101 = hunderteins. A thousand is «tausend». Phone numbers are usually read digit by digit.
topicos.comparacao: English says "twenty-five", tens first. German says "five-and-twenty", ones first. When you hear a number, wait for the end: in «sechsundachtzig», the 8 comes last, and it's the biggest part.

erros.motivo: The ones come first, joined by «und».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: look at the numbers. STEP 2: look at the times. STEP 3: look at the dates.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.explicacao: Questions: «Wie spät ist es?» or «Wie viel Uhr ist es?» (What time is it?). Answer: «Es ist acht Uhr.» For the time something happens: «Um wie viel Uhr?» — «Um acht Uhr» (at eight). In everyday speech: «fünf nach acht» (8:05, five past eight), «Viertel nach acht» (8:15, quarter past), «halb neun» (8:30), «Viertel vor neun» (8:45, quarter to), «fünf vor neun» (8:55). Careful: «halb neun» means HALF AN HOUR BEFORE nine, so 8:30. British "half nine" means 9:30 — the opposite! In official contexts (trains, TV) the 24-hour clock is used: «acht Uhr dreißig», «vierzehn Uhr fünfzehn».
topicos.comparacao: English "half past eight" looks back at the hour that has passed. German «halb neun» looks ahead to the hour that's coming, nine. «Viertel nach» and «Viertel vor» work just like "quarter past" and "quarter to".

erros.motivo: «halb drei» is half an hour before three: 2:30.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.titulo: Days of the week, months and the date
topicos.explicacao: Days and months are all masculine (der Montag, der Januar) — and like all nouns, capitalized. «Am» + day = on (Monday): «am Montag». «Im» + month = in (January): «im Mai». The date uses an ordinal with a period: «der 5. Oktober» (der fünfte Oktober) — the period does the job of English "th". Up to 19, the ordinal is the number + -te (der vierte); 1, 3, 7 and 8 are special (erste, dritte, siebte, achte), as in first, third. From 20 on, it's the number + -ste (der zwanzigste). In «am 5. Oktober», read «am fünften Oktober». The day comes before the month: 5.10. is October 5th.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Numbers, time and days
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest mistake is reading halb drei as "half past three" (and showing up an hour late!). British speakers are hit twice, because "half three" means 3:30. The other one: the time prepositions — um for clock times (at eight), am for days and dates (on Monday), im for months and seasons (in May). STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: Halb looks ahead: halb fünf = half an hour before five = 4:30.
Ones first, then und, then the tens — all in one word.

erros.errado: Der Kurs beginnt am vier Uhr.
erros.certo: Der Kurs beginnt um vier Uhr.

erros.motivo: Months take im ("in"); days and dates take am ("on").
Days are nouns, so they're capitalized.
With Jahre, add alt — like "years old".

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: German marks the role on the article — but only in the masculine. That's the whole trap: STEP 2: only the masculine changes. So just ask whether the word is a der word. If it isn't, nothing happens.
topicos.comparacao: English works out who does what from word order: "the man sees the dog" and "the dog sees the man" are different because the order changes — "the" never changes. German keeps the order freer and marks the object on the article instead: «Den Hund sieht der Mann» still means "the man sees the dog". You already know the idea from English pronouns: he sees → sees him. German does the same with masculine articles: der → den.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.titulo: The accusative: the direct object changes only in the masculine
topicos.explicacao: German has four cases. For now you need two: the NOMINATIVE (who does the action) and the ACCUSATIVE (the direct object: what you eat, drink, buy or have). The only difference between them is in the MASCULINE singular: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen. Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same. Verbs that take the accusative: essen, trinken, kaufen, haben, nehmen, möchten, lesen, sehen.
topicos.comparacao: English "the" never changes: "the cheese" is the same as subject or object. German changes only the masculine: «der Käse» (subject) × «den Käse» (object) — the same switch as he → him.

tabela.exemplo: Ich esse den Käse. Ich trinke einen Saft.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: compare the sentences. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: which gender changes form when it goes from subject to object? STEP 4: what happens to ein in the masculine? STEP 5: who is the subject in Ich kaufe den Tisch? And the object?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.titulo: Verbs that change e to i or ie
topicos.explicacao: A group of very common verbs changes the vowel «e» to «i» or «ie» with «du» and «er / sie / es»: essen → du isst, er isst. The other persons are regular. In «nehmen» a consonant changes too (nimmst, nimmt). Learn each of these verbs with its «du» and «er» forms — the way English learners memorize irregular verbs.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.explicacao: «Ich möchte» is "I'd like" — more polite than «ich will», which is closer to "I want" (and never means "I will"!). The modal verb goes in 2nd position and the other verb goes to the END, in the infinitive: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken» — literally "I'd like a coffee drink". This is the sentence "bracket". If the meaning is clear, the second verb can be left out: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee.» To order: «Ich nehme …» (I'll have …), «Ich möchte …», «Die Rechnung, bitte» and «Zahlen, bitte» (the check, please).
topicos.comparacao: English keeps the verbs together: "I'd like to drink a coffee". German splits them and sends the second verb to the end: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken». And there's no "to": just the infinitive.

erros.motivo: The second verb goes to the END of the sentence.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Food and drink
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest mistake is forgetting the -en of the masculine object (Ich habe ein Hund instead of einen Hund), because English "a" never changes. Then the overcorrection: putting the accusative after sein (Das ist einen Tisch instead of ein Tisch), and calling every thing «es», like English "it" (Ich kaufe es for der Computer instead of ihn). STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: English "a" never changes; German masculine ein becomes einen as an object.
Masculine object: der → den, like he → him.
A masculine thing is ihn, not es — even though English says "it".
After sein there's no object: the nominative stays.
With möchten, the second verb goes to the end.
essen changes e → i with du and er: du isst, er isst.

topicos.aulaTitulo: My daily routine
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: a separable prefix goes to the end. Be-, ge-, er-, ver-, ent-, emp- stay attached.
topicos.comparacao: English speakers have a head start here: phrasal verbs. "I get up", "I call you back", "the bus pulls in" — English already splits verb and particle. German goes further: the prefix flies to the very END of the sentence, however long it is. «Ich rufe dich morgen um acht Uhr an» — "I call you tomorrow at eight up". Three traps: forgetting to send it to the end, leaving it in the middle (like English "get off at Marienplatz"), and splitting verbs that never split.

tabela.alemao: Der Bus fährt um zehn Uhr ab.

topicos.aulaTitulo: My daily routine
topicos.titulo: Separable verbs: the prefix goes to the end
topicos.explicacao: Many German verbs have a prefix that splits off: «aufstehen» (to get up). In the present, the conjugated verb sits in 2nd position and the PREFIX goes to the END of the sentence: «Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf» — like "I get up at seven", but with "up" at the very end. In the infinitive, or with a modal verb, the verb stays whole: «Ich möchte um sieben Uhr aufstehen.» Common separable prefixes: auf- (up), an- (on, at), ein- (in), mit- (with, along), ab- (off, away), fern- (far), aus- (out), zurück- (back) — often the same ideas as English particles. Other prefixes NEVER separate: be-, ge-, er-, ver-, zer-, ent-, emp-: «Ich besuche meine Oma» (besuchen).
topicos.comparacao: English phrasal verbs ("get up", "call back") already split verb and particle, but the particle usually stays close to the verb. In German it goes to the end of the clause, and the whole sentence is "bracketed" between the verb and the prefix.

tabela.exemplo: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.

tabela.pt: She watches TV in the evening.

tabela.exemplo: Der Zug kommt um acht Uhr an.

erros.certo: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
erros.motivo: The separable prefix goes to the end of the sentence.

topicos.aulaTitulo: My daily routine
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: look at the verbs. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: in sentence 1, where is auf? And the verb stehe? STEP 4: in sentence 4, with the modal, what happens to aufstehen? STEP 5: in sentence 5, where is auf? STEP 6: in sentences 6 and 7, do the prefixes ver- and be- split off? STEP 7: in sentence 2, the verb is fährt. Which vowel change do you notice?

topicos.aulaTitulo: My daily routine
topicos.titulo: Verbs with a → ä, and how to say when
topicos.explicacao: Some verbs change «a» to «ä» with «du» and «er / sie / es»: fahren (du fährst), schlafen (du schläfst), laufen (du läufst), waschen (du wäschst), tragen (du trägst). To say WHEN: «um» + clock time (um sieben Uhr — at seven), «am» + part of the day (am Morgen, am Mittag, am Abend — but «in der Nacht», at night), «von … bis» (von neun bis siebzehn Uhr — from nine to five), «jeden Tag» (every day) and the adverbs «morgens, mittags, abends, nachts» for things you do regularly — like English "mornings", "evenings".

linhas.exemplo: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
Ich arbeite von neun bis siebzehn Uhr.

topicos.aulaTitulo: My daily routine
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest mistakes: keeping the prefix glued to the conjugated verb (Ich anrufe dich instead of Ich rufe dich an); leaving it in the middle, where English puts its particle (Wir steigen aus am Marienplatz, from "we get off at Marienplatz"); splitting inseparable verbs (be-, ge-, er-, ver-, ent-, emp-); or splitting after a modal verb. STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: The conjugated verb goes in position 2; the prefix an goes to the end.
Not where English puts "off": the prefix goes to the very end.
Question: verb first, prefix still at the end.
After a modal, the infinitive stays whole, at the end.
be- is inseparable: it never splits.
bekommen = to get, receive — "to become" is werden.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Town and directions
topicos.explicacao: With «in», German separates WHERE you are (Wo?) from WHERE you're going (Wohin?) — the way English separates "in" from "into", or old English "where" from "whither". Wo? uses the DATIVE: masculine and neuter «im» (in dem), feminine «in der». Wohin? uses the ACCUSATIVE: masculine «in den», feminine «in die», neuter «ins» (in das). To go to a place there's also «zu» (always dative): zum (zu dem) Bahnhof, zur (zu der) Post; and «nach» for cities and countries: nach Berlin. The full cases come in lessons 11 to 13; for now, memorize the chart.
topicos.comparacao: English changes the preposition: "I'm in the park" vs "I'm going into / to the park". German keeps the same preposition («in») and changes the article instead: «im Park» (in) vs «in den Park» (into). And "to" has three German versions: «in» for buildings you enter, «zu» for people and places you go up to, «nach» for cities and countries.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Town and directions
topicos.titulo: Asking for and giving directions (formal imperative)
topicos.explicacao: To ask: «Entschuldigung, wo ist die Post?» (Excuse me, where's the post office?) or «Wie komme ich zum Bahnhof?» (How do I get to the station?). To answer, use the formal imperative: the verb comes FIRST, followed by «Sie»: «Gehen Sie geradeaus.» (Go straight ahead.) «Biegen Sie links ab.» (Turn left — «abbiegen» is separable, so the prefix goes to the end.) «Nehmen Sie die zweite Straße rechts.» (Take the second street on the right.) English drops the "you" in commands; German formal commands keep «Sie». Other useful phrases: an der Ampel (at the light), an der Kreuzung (at the intersection), neben (next to), gegenüber (across from), in der Nähe (nearby).

tabela.frase: Gehen Sie geradeaus.
Biegen Sie links ab.
Biegen Sie rechts ab.
Nehmen Sie die zweite Straße links.
tabela.pt: Take the second street on the left.

tabela.frase: An der Ampel links.
Das ist nicht weit.
Es ist neben der Bank.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Review and test of the first block
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: there's a second trap. Modern English uses "where" for three ideas. German keeps them apart: STEP 2: wo for staying put, wohin for movement towards, woher for movement from — the old English "where, whither, whence".
topicos.comparacao: English builds questions with "do": "Do you live in Munich?" German has no "do" at all: the verb itself moves to first position — Wohnst du in München? Think of English "Are you…?" or "Can you…?", where the verb already comes first, and do the same with every verb.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Review and test of the first block
topicos.titulo: Everything you already know, in one table
topicos.explicacao: This table sums up lessons 1 to 9, one line per point. Reread one line at a time and say an example of your own out loud. If something feels odd, go back to the lesson shown or open the topic in the Grammar tab.

tabela.regra: ei = "eye", ie = long "ee", sch = "sh", ch = soft "kh" (ich) or throaty (Bach), w = "v", v = "f", z = "ts", s + vowel = "z".
The conjugated verb goes in 2nd position; a yes/no question starts with the verb — never with "do".
ich bin, du bist, er ist...; ich habe, du hast, er hat...
du (one friend), ihr (several friends), Sie (formal, one or several).
der, die, das; every noun capitalized; learn the article with the word.
Five patterns: -e, -(e)n, -er, no ending, -s (often with an umlaut).
ein Tisch, eine Lampe, kein Buch; in the plural, keine.
-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en; stem in -t or -d: du arbeitest.
mein, meine…: they agree with the thing owned.
21 = einundzwanzig (unidade + und + dezena).
«halb neun» = 8h30; Viertel vor / nach.
am Montag, im Mai, der 5. Oktober.
Only the masculine changes: der → den, ein → einen, kein → keinen.
du isst, er liest, du nimmst.
ich möchte … + second verb in the infinitive, at the end.
Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.
du fährst, er schläft.
im Park (dative) × in den Park (accusative).
Gehen Sie geradeaus!

topicos.aulaTitulo: Review and test of the first block
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: compare the questions and answers. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: where is the verb in questions without a question word? STEP 4: where is the verb in questions with a question word? Can the subject disappear in the answer?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Review and test of the first block
topicos.explicacao: These ten mistakes show up most often in English speakers. Fixing just these makes your German sound far more natural. Read each pair out loud: first the wrong one (to recognize how odd it sounds), then the right one.

erros.motivo: Same as English: "I am 20 years old" — but don't drop alt after Jahre.
No "do": the verb itself opens the question.
No "am …-ing": one verb form covers both.
One "the" in English, three in German: learn the article with the word.
Capital letter at the start and on every noun; languages too, as in English.
The second verb goes to the end.
A masculine thing is ihn, not "it" = es.
The separable prefix goes to the very end, not where English puts "off".
halb looks ahead: half an hour BEFORE three (British "half three" is the opposite).

topicos.aulaTitulo: Review and test of the first block
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest mistakes: using wo for everything, because English "where" covers all three (a destination needs wohin, an origin woher); keeping the subject before the verb in a question (Wo du wohnst? instead of Wo wohnst du?); looking for a "do" that German doesn't have; and mixing up wer ("who") with "where". STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: English "where" covers three ideas; a destination needs wohin.
Question word first, then the verb, then the subject.
No "do" in German: the verb itself opens the question.
Verb right after the question word.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Können and möchten: ability, permission, requests and invitations
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: nicht müssen = don't have to. Nicht dürfen = mustn't (forbidden). English "must not" sounds like «muss nicht», but it means «darf nicht» — mixing them up flips the meaning.
topicos.comparacao: Three traps, and they're all false friends: «ich will» means "I want", never "I will"; «ich muss nicht» means "I don't have to", not "I must not"; and «ich darf nicht» is the real "I mustn't / I'm not allowed".

topicos.aulaTitulo: Können and möchten: ability, permission, requests and invitations
topicos.titulo: Können: your first modal verb, step by step
topicos.explicacao: A MODAL verb helps another verb say "can", "must", "should", "want to". Let's build the first one, «können» — a cousin of English "can". STEP 1: «können» says what you know how to do or are able to do: «Ich kann schwimmen» = I can swim. STEP 2: conjugate «können»; it's irregular in the singular: ich kann, du kannst, er kann, wir können, ihr könnt, sie können. STEP 3: the second verb goes to the END of the sentence, in the infinitive: «Ich kann gut schwimmen» — "I can well swim". The sentence is "bracketed": the modal in 2nd position and the infinitive at the end. STEP 4: to ask, the modal goes to the front: «Kannst du schwimmen?» — exactly like "Can you swim?". STEP 5: to negate, «nicht» goes before the verb at the end: «Ich kann nicht schwimmen.» RULE OF THUMB: «ich» and «er» are the SAME (kann) and never take -t — just as English says "I can, he can", never "he cans".
topicos.comparacao: English modals work almost the same way: "I can swim", "Can you swim?", and "he can" with no -s, just like «er kann» with no -t. The one big difference is position: in German, the infinitive always goes to the END of the sentence instead of staying next to the modal. «Ich kann sehr gut Deutsch sprechen» — "I can very well German speak".

exemplos.ru: Kannst du Klavier spielen? — Ja, ein bisschen.
exemplos.pt: Can you play the piano? — Yes, a little.

erros.motivo: With «er», the modal takes no -t — like "he can", not "he cans".
The main verb goes to the END of the sentence.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Können and möchten: ability, permission, requests and invitations
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: look at the bracket. STEP 2: look at the verb können too. STEP 3: Questions: STEP 4: where is the modal in the sentence? And the main verb? STEP 5: compare ich kann and er kann. What do you notice? What's the difference between sentences 4 and 5?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Können and möchten: ability, permission, requests and invitations
topicos.titulo: Asking for help and for explanations
topicos.explicacao: «Kannst du …?» (informal) and «Können Sie …?» (formal) are the most common ways to ask for something — like "Can you…?" / "Could you…?". The main verb goes to the END, in the infinitive. Learn these classroom phrases: they work in any conversation with a German speaker and already show up in A1 exams. «langsamer» means "more slowly" — the -er works like English -er.

tabela.frase: Wie bitte?
Können Sie das bitte wiederholen?
Können Sie bitte langsamer sprechen?
tabela.pt: Could you speak more slowly, please?

tabela.frase: Ich verstehe das nicht.
Was bedeutet «Bahnhof»?
Wie schreibt man das?
Können Sie das buchstabieren?
Wie sagt man «obrigado» auf Deutsch?
tabela.pt: How do you say "thank you" in German?

tabela.frase: Können Sie mir helfen?

erros.motivo: The main verb goes to the end.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Können and möchten: ability, permission, requests and invitations
topicos.explicacao: To invite someone, use «Möchtest du …?» (informal) or «Möchten Sie …?» (formal) — "Would you like to…?" — or «Kannst du …?» for a request («Kannst du um acht Uhr kommen?»). To ACCEPT: «Ja, gern!», «Gute Idee!», «Ja, das kann ich.» To DECLINE politely, say «leider» (unfortunately) and give a reason: «Nein, leider nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.» Always start with the word that answers: «Ja» or «Nein».

tabela.exemplo: Möchtest du am Samstag ins Kino gehen?
Ja, gern! / Gute Idee! / Ja, das kann ich.
Nein, leider nicht. / Tut mir leid, ich kann nicht.
Ich habe keine Zeit. / Ich muss arbeiten.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Können and möchten: ability, permission, requests and invitations
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest mistakes: keeping the infinitive next to the modal, as in English (Ich kann sprechen Deutsch instead of Ich kann Deutsch sprechen); adding "to" (Ich möchte zu essen); reading «ich will» as "I will" (it's "I want"); and the biggest false friend — «muss nicht» means "don't have to", while English "must not" is «darf nicht». STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: The infinitive goes to the end, not next to the modal as in English.

erros.errado: Du musst hier nicht parken. (= you mustn't)
erros.motivo: English "must not" = darf nicht; muss nicht = don't have to.

erros.errado: Ich will morgen kommen. (= I will)
erros.certo: Ich komme morgen. / Ich werde morgen kommen.

erros.motivo: Like "he can": no ending on the modal with er.

erros.errado: Ich möchte zu essen einen Kuchen.
erros.motivo: No "to" after a modal; infinitive at the end.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Müssen, wollen and dürfen: obligation, wish and permission
topicos.titulo: Müssen: obligation and necessity, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «müssen» expresses what you HAVE TO do (obligation or necessity): «Ich muss arbeiten» = I have to work / I must work — "must" is its English cousin. STEP 2: conjugate: ich muss, du musst, er muss, wir müssen, ihr müsst, sie müssen. The «ü» disappears in the singular and, as with «können», «ich» and «er» are the same, with no -t. STEP 3: the second verb goes to the END, in the infinitive: «Du musst pünktlich sein.» STEP 4: question: «Muss ich heute arbeiten?» STEP 5: a separable verb stays WHOLE at the end: «Ich muss um sieben Uhr aufstehen.» English needs "have to" (two words plus "to"); German has one modal and no "to".
topicos.comparacao: English says "I have to work" or "I must work". German only has the second pattern: «Ich muss arbeiten», with the infinitive at the end of the sentence. And remember the trap from lesson 11: «Ich muss nicht» means "I don't have to", not "I mustn't".

erros.errado: Ich muss aufstehe um sieben Uhr.
erros.certo: Ich muss um sieben Uhr aufstehen.
erros.motivo: The whole infinitive goes to the end.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Müssen, wollen and dürfen: obligation, wish and permission
topicos.titulo: Wollen: want to, and how it differs from möchten
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «wollen» expresses a FIRM wish or a plan: «Ich will nächste Woche nach Berlin fahren» = I want to go to Berlin next week. False friend alert: «ich will» never means "I will". STEP 2: conjugate: ich will, du willst, er will, wir wollen, ihr wollt, sie wollen. Careful: «ich» and «er» are both «will», with no -t. STEP 3: the infinitive goes to the end. STEP 4: «möchten» is softer and more polite ("I'd like"); «wollen» is direct ("I want"). When asking a stranger for something, prefer «möchten»: «Ich möchte einen Kaffee», not «Ich will einen Kaffee», which sounds curt — just like "I want a coffee" does in English.

linhas.exemplo: Ich will heute Abend zu Hause bleiben.

erros.errado: Ich will einen Kaffee, bitte. (at a café, to a stranger)

topicos.aulaTitulo: Müssen, wollen and dürfen: obligation, wish and permission
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «dürfen» expresses PERMISSION: «Darf ich hier sitzen?» = May I sit here? STEP 2: conjugate: ich darf, du darfst, er darf, wir dürfen, ihr dürft, sie dürfen (the «ü» disappears in the singular). STEP 3: with «nicht», «dürfen» means FORBIDDEN — it's the German "mustn't": «Hier darf man nicht rauchen» = you mustn't smoke here. STEP 4: «man» is impersonal, like English "one" or the general "you": «Hier darf man parken» (you can park here). It takes the «er» form of the verb. Signs use the infinitive or a noun: «Rauchen verboten», «Parken erlaubt», «Eingang», «Ausgang».

erros.motivo: The subject «man» is missing; it takes the form «darf».
Question: the modal comes first and «ich» takes «darf».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Müssen, wollen and dürfen: obligation, wish and permission
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest mistakes: «muss nicht» used for English "mustn't" (that's «darf nicht»); «ich will» used for "I will" (it means "I want"); «wollen» in a shop, where it sounds as curt as "I want…" (use «möchten»); the infinitive next to the modal, as in English; and an -t on the modal with er (er kannt, er willt). STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.errado: Hier muss man nicht rauchen. (= you mustn't smoke)
erros.motivo: "Mustn't" = darf nicht; muss nicht = don't have to.

erros.errado: Ich will morgen anrufen. (= I will call)
erros.motivo: «ich will» = I want; for the future, the present tense is enough.

erros.errado: Ich will einen Kaffee. (to a waiter)
erros.motivo: «wollen» sounds curt in a shop; use «möchten».
ich and er are the same: no -t.

erros.errado: Ich muss aufstehen um sieben Uhr.
erros.certo: Ich muss um sieben Uhr aufstehen.
erros.motivo: The infinitive goes to the end.
Impersonal "you" needs «man», with the er form.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the vowel changes only with du and er/sie/es. With ich, wir, ihr and sie, the verb stays as in the infinitive.
topicos.comparacao: Three traps. English has one command form for everyone ("Speak slowly!"); German has three, depending on who you're talking to — and the du form keeps the vowel change.

tabela.ingles: Speak slowly! (to a group of friends)

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.titulo: The imperative with «Sie» and «wir», step by step
topicos.explicacao: The imperative is for asking, giving instructions, inviting and telling people what to do. We start with the POLITE form, which you hear in shops, schools and exams. STEP 1: take the infinitive («öffnen») and put «Sie» after it: «Öffnen Sie das Buch.» So the verb comes FIRST and «Sie» right behind it. English drops the "you" in commands; German formal commands keep it. STEP 2: separable verbs: the prefix goes to the END: «Hören Sie zu.», «Stehen Sie auf.» STEP 3: «bitte» makes the request polite and can go in several places: «Öffnen Sie bitte das Buch.» STEP 4: the «wir» form invites people to do something together — the German "let's": «Gehen wir!» (Let's go!), «Fangen wir an!» (Let's begin!). STEP 5: to negate, put «nicht» at the end: «Rauchen Sie nicht!»
topicos.comparacao: English commands drop the subject: "Open the book." The German formal imperative keeps it, right after the verb: «Öffnen Sie das Buch» — almost a question without the question mark. And "let's…" is simply the wir form with the verb first: «Gehen wir!»

erros.motivo: In the imperative, the verb comes BEFORE «Sie».
The separable prefix goes to the end.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: look at the verbs. STEP 2: now look at the commands. STEP 3: Questions: STEP 4: in which persons does the vowel change? In which doesn't it? STEP 5: compare du sprichst and Sprich!. What happened to the -st? Is the i still there? STEP 6: compare du fährst and Fahr!. Is the ä still there? STEP 7: where is the verb in sentences 5, 6 and 7?

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.titulo: The imperative with «du» and «ihr», step by step
topicos.explicacao: With friends, family and children you use «du» (one person) or «ihr» (several). STEP 1, «du»: take the du form of the present, drop «du» and the «-st»: «du kommst» → «Komm!» STEP 2: if the verb changes e to i or ie in the present, the imperative KEEPS the change: «du nimmst» → «Nimm!», «du sprichst» → «Sprich!», «du liest» → «Lies!», «du gibst» → «Gib!», «du hilfst» → «Hilf!» STEP 3: if the verb has an umlaut (a → ä), the imperative has NO umlaut: «du fährst» → «Fahr!» STEP 4: a stem in -t or -d adds -e: «Warte!» STEP 5, «ihr»: it's the present form without «ihr»: «Kommt!», «Wartet!» STEP 6: «sein» is irregular: «Sei ruhig!» (du), «Seid ruhig!» (ihr), «Seien Sie ruhig!» (Sie) — compare English "Be quiet!". Separable verbs: «Steh auf!», «Steht auf!»

erros.motivo: The imperative has no umlaut (a → ä only in the present).

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.titulo: The phrases in exams and textbooks
topicos.explicacao: German textbooks and exams, from A1 to B1, give their instructions in the formal imperative. Learning these phrases now saves you from losing points just because you didn't understand the task. They all follow what you've seen: verb first, «Sie» after, separable prefix at the end.

tabela.frase: Lesen Sie den Text.
Hören Sie das Gespräch.
Kreuzen Sie an: richtig oder falsch.
tabela.pt: Mark true or false with an X.

tabela.frase: Ergänzen Sie die Sätze.
Beantworten Sie die Fragen.
Schreiben Sie eine E-Mail.
Ordnen Sie die Wörter.
Markieren Sie das Beispiel.

topicos.aulaTitulo: The imperative: asking, telling and instructing
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest mistakes: using one command form for everyone, as in English (Sprich! to your boss, or Sprechen Sie! to your kid); dropping the vowel change in du and er/sie/es (du sprechst, er nehmt); changing the vowel where it doesn't belong (ich fähre); leaving the -st or -t in the du imperative (Gibst / Gibt mir! instead of Gib mir!); and looking for a "don't" — German just adds nicht. STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: English has one command form; German needs the formal one with Sie.
sprechen changes e → i with du and er.
The du imperative drops the ending: Gib!
ich never takes the vowel change.
No "don't" in German: just add nicht.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: a second trap: English uses "not … any" where German uses one word: "I don't have any time" = «Ich habe keine Zeit», "I don't have anything" = «Ich habe nichts». No "do", no "not … any". STEP 2: is there an ein (or no article) in the positive sentence? Swap it for kein. Otherwise, use nicht.
topicos.comparacao: English negates with "not" and usually needs "do": "I don't live in Berlin. I don't have a car. I don't have time." German has no "do" at all, and it splits the work between two words: «nicht» for verbs, places and adjectives, and «kein» — literally "no", as in "I have no car" — for nouns.

tabela.regra: negates the verb or the place: nicht
negates a noun with ein or no article: kein
same: kein
negates an adjective: nicht

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the DIRECT OBJECT is what receives the action: in «Ich sehe den Mann», the one I see is «den Mann». STEP 2: to avoid repeating the noun, we replace the object with a pronoun: «Ich sehe den Mann» → «Ich sehe ihn» (I see him). STEP 3: for things, the pronoun follows the noun's GENDER, where English always says "it": «der Tisch» → «ihn»; «die Lampe» → «sie»; «das Buch» → «es»; «die Bücher» → «sie». STEP 4: English already does this with people: I → me, he → him, we → us. German does the same: «ich» → «mich», «du» → «dich», «er» → «ihn», «wir» → «uns», «ihr» → «euch». STEP 5: careful with «sie» (her, them) and «Sie» (you, formal): context and the capital letter tell you which is which.
topicos.comparacao: English object pronouns are the closest match in the whole lesson: me, you, him, her, it, us, them. German has the same idea — mich, dich, ihn, sie, es, uns, euch, sie — with one twist: a thing gets «ihn» or «sie» according to its gender, never automatically "it".

exemplos.ru: Wo ist der Schlüssel? Ich suche ihn.
exemplos.pt: Where's the key? I'm looking for it.

exemplos.ru: Wo ist die Tasche? Ich finde sie nicht.
exemplos.pt: Where's the bag? I can't find it.

exemplos.ru: Das Buch ist gut. Ich lese es gern.
exemplos.pt: The book is good. I like reading it.

erros.motivo: A direct object takes the accusative — like he → him.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: compare each pair. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: when does ein, or no article, become kein? STEP 4: when does nicht appear? STEP 5: where is nicht when the sentence has no adjective or place?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.titulo: «Kein» and «keine»: negating a noun, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «kein» negates NOUNS — it's the English "no" in "I have no car", or "not a / not any". Use it instead of «ein», or when the noun has no article: «Ich habe ein Auto» → «Ich habe kein Auto»; «Ich habe Zeit» → «Ich habe keine Zeit». STEP 2: «kein» takes the endings of «ein»: masculine kein (nominative) and keinen (accusative); feminine keine; neuter kein; plural keine. STEP 3: set phrases with «haben»: «Ich habe keinen Hunger» (I'm not hungry — German "has" hunger), «keinen Durst», «keine Zeit», «keine Lust» (I don't feel like it), «keine Ahnung» (no idea). STEP 4: remember the masculine direct object takes -en: «keinen Hunger», «keinen Kaffee».

erros.motivo: «Hunger» is masculine: as a direct object → keinen.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.titulo: «Nicht»: where it goes, and answering with «doch»
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «kein» negates NOUNS; «nicht» negates EVERYTHING ELSE: the verb, the whole sentence, an adjective or an adverb. STEP 2: when it negates the whole sentence, «nicht» goes to the END: «Ich arbeite heute nicht» (I'm not working today). STEP 3: when it negates an adjective or adverb, it goes BEFORE it: «Das Buch ist nicht teuer.» STEP 4: with a separable verb, «nicht» comes before the prefix: «Ich stehe nicht auf.» STEP 5: with modals, before the infinitive: «Ich kann nicht kommen.» STEP 6: if someone asks a NEGATIVE question («Hast du keine Zeit?»), answer «DOCH» to mean "yes, I do" and «Nein» to mean "no, I don't". English has to say "Yes, I do!" with stress; German has one word, «doch», just for contradicting a negative.

tabela.exemplo: Hast du keine Zeit? — Doch, ich habe Zeit!
Hast du keine Zeit? — Nein, ich habe keine Zeit.

erros.errado: Hast du keine Zeit? — Ja, ich habe Zeit.
erros.certo: Hast du keine Zeit? — Doch, ich habe Zeit.
erros.motivo: To contradict a negative, use «doch», not «ja».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Accusative pronouns and negation (kein and nicht)
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the costliest mistakes: looking for a "do" (there is none); putting nicht before the verb, where English puts "not" (Ich nicht wohne); saying nicht ein for "not a" instead of kein (Das ist nicht ein Tisch); answering ja to a negative question when you mean "yes, I do" (it's doch); and saying es for every thing, like "it" (Ich suche es for der Schlüssel instead of ihn). STEP 2: read the table and say each correct sentence out loud before you look at the reason.

erros.motivo: No "do", and nicht doesn't go before the verb as "not" does in English.
"Not a" before a noun is kein(e).
"No time / not any time" = keine Zeit.

erros.errado: Hast du keine Zeit? — Ja, ich habe Zeit!
erros.motivo: To contradict a negative question, use doch.

erros.errado: Wo ist der Schlüssel? Ich suche es.
erros.motivo: A masculine thing is ihn, not "it" = es.
A job is a noun: negate it with kein(e).

topicos.aulaTitulo: Shopping and clothes
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: to describe something with «sein», the adjective comes AFTER the verb and does NOT change: «Die Jacke ist blau», «Die Schuhe sind schwarz» — exactly like English "the jacket is blue", "the shoes are black". STEP 2: ask «Welche Farbe hat …?» (what color is …?) or «Wie ist …?». STEP 3: colors are written in lowercase, because they're adjectives. STEP 4: the adjective can take «zu» (too): «Die Hose ist zu groß» (the pants are too big). Adjective endings in front of a noun (ein blaues Hemd) only come at A2; for now, use the adjective ON ITS OWN, after «sein».
topicos.comparacao: Good news: after «sein», German adjectives behave exactly like English ones — no ending at all: «ist blau», «sind blau», "is blue", "are blue". Several colors are almost English: braun (brown), grün (green), grau (gray), weiß (white).

topicos.aulaTitulo: Shopping and clothes
topicos.titulo: Asking the price, reading prices, and saying "too"
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: for the price, ask «Was kostet …?» or «Wie viel kostet …?» for ONE thing; for several, «Was kosten …?»: «Was kostet die Jacke?», «Was kosten die Schuhe?» — like "How much is…?" / "How much are…?". STEP 2: read prices like this: «25 €» = «fünfundzwanzig Euro»; «2,50 €» = «zwei Euro fünfzig» (euros first, then cents — and a comma, not a period); «0,99 €» = «neunundneunzig Cent». STEP 3: «zu» + adjective = too: «Die Hose ist zu groß.» STEP 4: size: «Größe 38», «Größe M» (European sizes: a US women's 8 is about a 38). STEP 5: three shop phrases: «Kann ich das anprobieren?» (Can I try this on?), «Haben Sie das in Größe M?», «Ich nehme das» (I'll take it). STEP 6: «passen» takes the person in the DATIVE: «Die Jacke passt mir» = the jacket fits me; treat it as a set phrase for now.

exemplos.ru: Was kostet die Jacke? — Sie kostet neunzig Euro.
exemplos.pt: How much is the jacket? — It's ninety euros.

exemplos.ru: Was kosten die Schuhe? — Sie kosten achtzig Euro.
exemplos.pt: How much are the shoes? — They're eighty euros.

exemplos.ru: Die Hose ist zu groß. Haben Sie sie in Größe 38?
exemplos.pt: The pants are too big. Do you have them in size 38?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Shopping and clothes
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «dieser, diese, dieses» (this) follow gender, like «der, die, das»: «dieser Pullover» (m), «diese Jacke» (f), «dieses Hemd» (n), «diese Schuhe» (plural, "these"). STEP 2: the masculine direct object changes, as you've learned: «Ich nehme diesen Pullover» (accusative: dieser → diesen). Feminine, neuter and plural stay the same. STEP 3: use it to point at things in a store: «Wie finden Sie diese Jacke?» (What do you think of this jacket?), «Ich nehme dieses Hemd.»

topicos.aulaTitulo: Jobs and the workplace
topicos.titulo: Saying your job: no article, and the feminine in -in
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: with «sein» (and «werden»), the job comes WITHOUT an article: «Ich bin Lehrer», not «Ich bin ein Lehrer» — even though English says "I'm a teacher". STEP 2: the feminine usually adds -in to the masculine: Lehrer → Lehrerin, Student → Studentin, Kellner → Kellnerin. English mostly uses one word for both ("teacher", "doctor"); German almost always marks a woman's job with -in. STEP 3: some words also take an umlaut: Arzt → Ärztin, Koch → Köchin. STEP 4: questions: «Was sind Sie von Beruf?» (formal), «Was bist du von Beruf?» (informal) or «Was machst du beruflich?» — "What do you do (for a living)?". STEP 5: another way to say it: «Ich arbeite als Verkäufer» (I work as a salesperson), also without an article — just like "work as". Careful: «Krankenschwester» (female nurse) has a different masculine: «Krankenpfleger».
topicos.comparacao: The English reflex "I'm a teacher" produces «Ich bin ein Lehrer», which sounds wrong. German drops the article before a job (unless there's an adjective: «Er ist ein guter Lehrer»). And where English has gender-neutral job titles, German usually has two forms: Lehrer / Lehrerin.

tabela.exemplo: Ich bin Lehrer. / Sie ist Lehrerin.
Er ist Student. / Sie ist Studentin.

erros.motivo: No article before a job after «sein» — unlike "I'm a teacher".
For a woman, the form is «Ärztin».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Jobs and the workplace
topicos.titulo: Where you work, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: ask «Wo arbeitest du?» or «Wo arbeiten Sie?». STEP 2: to give the PLACE, use «in» and the forms you know from lesson 9: der and das words take «im» (im Büro, im Krankenhaus, im Geschäft); die words take «in der» (in der Schule, in der Fabrik, in der Praxis). STEP 3: to say WHO you work FOR, or at which company, use «bei» — English uses "at" or "for": «Ich arbeite bei Siemens» (I work at / for Siemens), «bei der Post», «bei der Bank». STEP 4: hours: «Ich arbeite von acht bis siebzehn Uhr» (from eight to five). STEP 5: ask «Wie lange arbeitest du?» (how long per day) and «Wann arbeitest du?» (what time). STEP 6: two common situations: «Ich bin arbeitslos» (I'm unemployed) and «Ich habe frei / Urlaub» (I'm off / on vacation). At A2 you'll see why it's «im» and «in der»; for now, memorize the pairs.

tabela.resposta: Ich arbeite im Büro. / in der Schule. / in der Fabrik.
tabela.pt: At the office. / At school. / At the factory.

tabela.resposta: Ich arbeite bei Siemens. / bei der Post.
tabela.pt: At Siemens. / At the post office.

tabela.resposta: Ja, sehr gern. / Nein, nicht so gern.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Home and housing: es gibt
topicos.titulo: «Es gibt»: saying what there is, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «es gibt» means "there is" or "there are": «Es gibt einen Balkon» = there's a balcony. STEP 2: «es gibt» is a FIXED phrase — literally "it gives" — and, unlike English "there is / there are", it never changes for the plural: «Es gibt zwei Zimmer» (there are two rooms). What exists goes into the ACCUSATIVE, so masculine nouns take «einen» or «keinen»: «Es gibt einen Garten», «Es gibt keinen Garten». Feminine, neuter and plural don't change: «Es gibt eine Küche», «Es gibt ein Bad». STEP 3: to ask: «Gibt es einen Balkon?» (Is there a balcony?) STEP 4: the difference from «haben»: «haben» has an owner («Die Wohnung hat einen Balkon» — the apartment has a balcony); «es gibt» just says something exists («In der Wohnung gibt es einen Balkon»). Both take the accusative.
topicos.comparacao: English switches between "there is" and "there are"; German «es gibt» never changes. And since «es gibt» is literally "it gives", what follows is an object — so the masculine changes: einen Balkon, keinen Garten.

tabela.exemplo: Es gibt einen Balkon. / Es gibt keinen Garten.
tabela.pt: There's a balcony. / There's no garden.
Is there a supermarket around here?

erros.motivo: What exists goes into the accusative: «Balkon» is masculine.
«es gibt» doesn't change, even in the plural — unlike "there are".

topicos.aulaTitulo: Home and housing: es gibt
topicos.titulo: Describing a home, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «haben» says what the home has: «Die Wohnung hat drei Zimmer.» STEP 2: ask «Wie viele Zimmer hat die Wohnung?» (How many rooms does the apartment have?) STEP 3: adjectives come after «sein» and don't change: «Die Küche ist klein und hell.» STEP 4: size, in square meters: «Die Wohnung hat sechzig Quadratmeter» (written 60 m²; about 650 sq ft). STEP 5: rent: «Die Miete kostet sechshundert Euro im Monat.» Careful: in German ads, «Zimmer» counts all rooms except kitchen and bathroom — a «2-Zimmer-Wohnung» is a living room plus one bedroom, not a two-bedroom. STEP 6: WHERE (Wo?) and WHERE TO (Wohin?), with the pairs from lesson 9: «im Wohnzimmer» / «ins Wohnzimmer»; «in der Küche» / «in die Küche»; «im Bad» / «ins Bad»; «im Garten» / «in den Garten». Careful: for the balcony, German uses «auf» ("on"), as English does: «auf dem Balkon» / «auf den Balkon».

exemplos.ru: Die Wohnung hat drei Zimmer und einen Balkon.
exemplos.pt: The apartment has three rooms and a balcony.

exemplos.ru: Die Küche ist klein, aber hell.
exemplos.pt: The kitchen is small but bright.

exemplos.ru: Ich bin in der Küche. Ich gehe ins Bad.
exemplos.pt: I'm in the kitchen. I'm going to the bathroom.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Home and housing: es gibt
topicos.explicacao: Ads are short and full of abbreviations. Learn the most common ones: «Zi.» or «-Zimmer-Wohnung» (rooms), «m²» (square meters, «Quadratmeter»), «€ / Monat» (euros per month), «NK» or «Nebenkosten» (extra costs: heating, water, trash, building fees), «ab sofort» (available now), «Balkon», «Bad», «Kü.» (kitchen). Sample ad (original): «Schöne 2-Zimmer-Wohnung, 55 m², Küche, Bad, Balkon. Miete 600 € im Monat plus Nebenkosten. Ab sofort frei.» In English: "Nice 2-room apartment (1 bedroom + living room), 55 m², kitchen, bathroom, balcony. Rent €600 a month plus utilities. Available now."

tabela.significado: extra costs: heating, water, trash, building fees

topicos.aulaTitulo: Free time, weather and hobbies
topicos.titulo: Gern, lieber, am liebsten: what I like and prefer
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: «gern» (gladly) goes AFTER the verb and says you like doing something: «Ich schwimme gern» — "I swim gladly" = I like swimming. German doesn't need a separate "like" verb here. STEP 2: «nicht gern» says you don't like it: «Ich koche nicht gern» (I don't like cooking). STEP 3: «lieber» says what you PREFER: «Ich lese lieber» (I'd rather read). STEP 4: «am liebsten» says what you like MOST: «Am liebsten tanze ich» (what I like best is dancing). The scale is: gern → lieber → am liebsten — like good → better → best, but for liking. STEP 5: useful questions: «Was machst du gern?» (What do you like doing?), «Was machst du am Wochenende?», «Was ist dein Hobby?» STEP 6: «Mein Hobby ist Fußball» (one) or «Meine Hobbys sind Lesen und Tanzen» (several).
topicos.comparacao: English says "I like swimming" with a like-verb plus -ing. German just adds «gern» to the verb you do: «Ich schwimme gern». And «lieber» is the old English "liefer" ("I'd as lief…"), meaning "rather" — German kept it.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Free time, weather and hobbies
topicos.titulo: Talking about the weather: the impersonal «es», step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: ask «Wie ist das Wetter?» (What's the weather like?) STEP 2: for rain and snow, German uses the verb with «es»: «Es regnet» (it's raining), «Es schneit» (it's snowing). The «es» is required and doesn't refer to anything — exactly like English "it". STEP 3: with adjectives: «Es ist warm / kalt / heiß / kühl / windig / sonnig / bewölkt» (it's warm / cold / hot / cool / windy / sunny / cloudy). STEP 4: temperature, in Celsius: «Es sind zwanzig Grad» (it's 20 degrees, about 68 °F) — note the plural «sind». STEP 5: the seasons are der words and take «im»: «im Frühling», «im Sommer», «im Herbst», «im Winter» (in spring, summer, fall, winter): «Im Sommer ist es heiß.» STEP 6: to say you feel cold, German says «Mir ist kalt» — "to me it is cold". «Ich bin kalt» would mean you're a cold person!

tabela.frase: Es regnet.
Es schneit.
Es ist sonnig und warm.
Es ist kalt und windig.
Es sind zwanzig Grad.
Im Winter ist es kalt.
Mir ist kalt.

erros.motivo: The impersonal «es» is missing — like "it" in "it's raining".
For how you feel, say «Mir ist kalt», not «ich bin» — that would mean you're a cold person.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Free time, weather and hobbies
topicos.explicacao: To suggest something: «Wollen wir …?» (shall we …?), «Hast du Lust auf …?» (do you feel like …?). After «Lust auf» comes a noun in the accusative: «Hast du Lust auf Kino?», «Lust auf ein Picknick?». To agree: «Gute Idee!», «Einverstanden!» (deal!). To suggest something else: «Dann …» (then …), «Oder …?» (or …?). For bad weather: «Bei Regen gehen wir ins Kino» (if it rains, we'll go to the movies).

tabela.exemplo: Wollen wir wandern gehen? / Hast du Lust auf Kino?
Nein, leider nicht. Ich muss arbeiten.
Dann gehen wir ins Kino. / Oder wollen wir Rad fahren?
Bei Regen bleiben wir zu Hause.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Travel and transport
topicos.titulo: How you get there: «mit» + means of transportation
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: for the MEANS, use «mit» + article — where English says "by bus", German says "with the bus": «mit dem Zug», «mit dem Bus», «mit dem Auto», «mit dem Fahrrad», «mit dem Flugzeug», «mit dem Taxi». For die words: «mit der U-Bahn», «mit der Straßenbahn». Learn them as ready-made chunks (why it's «dem» and «der» comes at A2). STEP 2: "on foot" is «zu Fuß», with no article. STEP 3: ask «Wie kommst du zur Arbeit?» (How do you get to work?) or «Wie fährst du?» STEP 4: «fahren» changes a to ä with «du» and «er» (du fährst, er fährt); «fliegen» and «gehen» are regular in the present. Careful: «gehen» means going on foot — if you take any vehicle, German says «fahren». STEP 5: the DESTINATION: «nach» with cities and countries («nach Berlin», «nach Kanada»); «zu» with places and people («zum Bahnhof», «zur Schule»).

tabela.frase: Ich fahre mit dem Zug.
Er fährt mit dem Bus zur Arbeit.

tabela.meio: das Auto / das Fahrrad / das Taxi
tabela.frase: Wir fahren mit dem Auto.
Sie fliegt mit dem Flugzeug nach Berlin.
Ich fahre mit der U-Bahn.
Ich gehe zu Fuß.

erros.motivo: The article is missing: "by train" is «mit dem Zug».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Travel and transport
topicos.titulo: Buying a ticket and reading the schedule, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: ask with «bitte»: «Eine Fahrkarte nach München, bitte» (a ticket to Munich, please). STEP 2: the clerk asks «Einfach oder hin und zurück?» (one-way or round-trip?). STEP 3: ask the time: «Wann fährt der Zug nach München?» and answer with «abfahren» (separable): «Der Zug fährt um vierzehn Uhr fünfzehn ab.» Arrival: «Er kommt um sechzehn Uhr an.» STEP 4: transportation schedules use the 24-hour clock, as in lesson 6 — 14:15 is 2:15 pm. STEP 5: «Von Gleis 5» (from track / platform 5). STEP 6: duration: «Wie lange dauert die Fahrt?» — «Drei Stunden.» STEP 7: changing trains: «Sie müssen in Frankfurt umsteigen» (you have to change in Frankfurt; separable).

tabela.frase: Eine Fahrkarte nach München, bitte.
Einfach oder hin und zurück?
Wann fährt der Zug nach München?
Der Zug fährt um 14.15 Uhr ab.
Er fährt von Gleis 5.
Die Fahrt dauert drei Stunden.
Sie müssen in Frankfurt umsteigen.

erros.errado: Der Zug abfährt um acht Uhr.
erros.certo: Der Zug fährt um acht Uhr ab.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Travel and transport
topicos.titulo: Booking a room, step by step
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: ask if they have a room: «Haben Sie ein Einzelzimmer frei?» or say: «Ich möchte ein Zimmer reservieren.» STEP 2: say how many nights: «Für zwei Nächte» («Nacht» has the plural «Nächte», like night → nights with an umlaut). STEP 3: ask the price: «Was kostet das Zimmer pro Nacht?» STEP 4: ask about breakfast: «Ist das Frühstück dabei?» (Is breakfast included?) STEP 5: payment: «Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?» STEP 6: at check-out: «Ich möchte bitte bezahlen.» Watch the floors: German counts like British English — «im zweiten Stock» is the second floor above the ground floor, so the THIRD floor in American terms.

tabela.frase: Haben Sie ein Einzelzimmer frei?
Für zwei Nächte, bitte.
Was kostet das Zimmer pro Nacht?
Ist das Frühstück dabei?
Kann ich mit Karte zahlen?

topicos.titulo: All of A1 in one table
topicos.explicacao: This table sums up lessons 1 to 19. Reread one line at a time and say an example of your own out loud. If a line feels odd, go back to the lesson shown or open the topic in the Grammar tab.

The conjugated verb goes in 2nd position; a yes/no question starts with the verb — no "do".
ich bin, du bist, er ist…; ich habe, du hast, er hat…

der, die, das; every noun capitalized; five plural patterns.
-e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en; stem in -t or -d: du arbeitest.
21 = einundzwanzig; halb neun = 8h30; am Montag, im Mai.

du isst, er liest; du fährst, er schläft.

topicos.aulaTitulo: A1 review and mock test
topicos.explicacao: Read each pair out loud: first the wrong one (to recognize how odd it sounds), then the right one. Fixing just these 14 makes your German far more natural.

erros.motivo: No "do" in German: the verb itself opens the question.
The second verb goes to the END.

erros.certo: Ich stehe um sieben Uhr auf.

erros.motivo: Accusative pronoun: he → him = er → ihn.
No article before a job — unlike "I'm a teacher".

erros.errado: Hier musst du nicht rauchen. (= you mustn't)
erros.motivo: English "mustn't" = darf nicht; muss nicht = don't have to.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: spoken past = auxiliary in position 2 + participle at the end. Movement or change of state = sein.
topicos.comparacao: Three traps. The FSI course, written for American diplomats in 1961, put it in capitals: German and English devices for talking about past time do not coincide exactly.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: the Perfekt is the past tense of CONVERSATION and messages: «Ich habe Deutsch gelernt». It looks like the English present perfect ("I have learned"), but it does the job of the simple past: «Gestern habe ich gearbeitet» = "I worked yesterday" — English would never say "Yesterday I have worked". STEP 2: it has TWO parts: the auxiliary «haben», conjugated, in 2nd position, and the PARTIZIP II (past participle) at the END of the sentence — the same bracket you know from the modals. STEP 3: the Partizip II of regular verbs is «ge-» + stem + «-t», like English "-ed": machen → gemacht; lernen → gelernt; spielen → gespielt; kaufen → gekauft; kochen → gekocht; hören → gehört. STEP 4: conjugate «haben»: ich habe, du hast, er hat, wir haben, ihr habt, sie haben. STEP 5: a yes/no question: «Hast du schon gegessen?» (Have you eaten yet? / Did you eat yet?) and the answer: «Ja, schon» or «Nein, noch nicht». STEP 6: use past time words: gestern, letzte Woche, letztes Jahr. And remember the opposite trap: "I've been living here for two years" is NOT a Perfekt in German — it's the present with «seit»: «Ich wohne seit zwei Jahren hier».
topicos.comparacao: English splits the past between "I did" and "I have done", and the choice matters. German conversation uses the Perfekt for both: «Ich habe gegessen» = "I ate" and "I have eaten". The form looks like English (have + participle), but the participle goes to the very END of the sentence.

erros.motivo: The Partizip II goes to the END of the sentence — not next to haben as in English.

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: look at the sentences. STEP 2: Questions: STEP 3: where are haben and sein in the sentence? And the participle? STEP 4: almost all participles start with ge-. In which sentences is the ge- "hidden"? Where does it show up? STEP 5: in sentences 4 and 5, which verbs take sein? What do aufstehen and kommen have in common? Compare gekocht and getrunken. Which ends in -t and which in -en?

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.titulo: Special cases of the regular Partizip II
topicos.explicacao: STEP 1: if the stem ends in -t or -d, the participle takes «-et» to stay pronounceable — just like English "waited", "needed": arbeiten → gearbeitet; warten → gewartet. STEP 2: verbs in «-ieren» take NO «ge-»: studieren → studiert; telefonieren → telefoniert; reparieren → repariert. These are mostly borrowed words you'll recognize (studieren, reparieren, informieren). STEP 3: verbs with an INSEPARABLE prefix (be-, ge-, er-, ver-, ent-, emp-, zer-) take NO «ge-» either: besuchen → besucht; bezahlen → bezahlt; verkaufen → verkauft; erklären → erklärt. STEP 4: rule of thumb: if the verb starts with be-, er-, ver-, ent- or ge-, or ends in -ieren, its participle has no «ge-». (The FSI's tip: «ge-» only goes on a verb whose FIRST syllable is stressed.)

tabela.regra: stem in -t / -d
stem in -t / -d
-ieren: no ge-
-ieren: no ge-
be-: no ge-
be-: no ge-
ver-: no ge-
er-: no ge-

erros.motivo: Stem in -t: the participle takes «-et», like "waited".
The prefix be- already takes the place of «ge-».

topicos.aulaTitulo: Perfekt 1: the past with haben (regular verbs)
topicos.titulo: Regular separable verbs: «ge-» goes in the middle
